The infinite-dimensionality of quantum mechanics is forced by one postulate and one line of linear algebra, before any physics has been done at all.

8.3 · How badly finite matrices fail, quantified

"Impossible" invites the response that some large matrix must come close, and the question deserves a number rather than a reassurance. It does not come close, and the bound is exact.

Use the inner product on matrices from Chapter 0.5 §1.2's table, ⟨A,B⟩=tr⁡(A†B)\avg{A,B}=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\dagger}B)⟨A,B⟩=tr(A†B), whose norm is ∥A∥F=(∑ij∣Aij∣2)1/2\norm{A}_{F}=\big(\sum_{ij}\abs{A_{ij}}^{2}\big)^{1/2}∥A∥F​=(∑ij​∣Aij​∣2)1/2. Apply Chapter 0.5 §1.4's Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in that space, to I^\hat II^ and any matrix MMM:

∣tr⁡M∣2  =  ∣⟨I^,M⟩∣2  ≤  ∥I^∥F2 ∥M∥F2  =  n ∥M∥F2. \abs{\operatorname{tr}M}^{2} \;=\; \abs{\avg{\hat I,M}}^{2} \;\le\; \norm{\hat I}_{F}^{2}\,\norm{M}_{F}^{2} \;=\; n\,\norm{M}_{F}^{2}. ∣trM∣2=​⟨I^,M⟩​2≤​I^​F2​∥M∥F2​=n∥M∥F2​. (4.2.25)

Now we want to apply that to the miss itself, so set M=[x^,p^]−iℏI^M=[\hat x,\hat p]-\ii\hbar\hat IM=[x^,p^​]−iℏI^, the amount by which a candidate pair fails. By (4.2.23) its trace is 0−iℏn0-\ii\hbar n0−iℏn, so ∣tr⁡M∣=ℏn\abs{\operatorname{tr}M}=\hbar n∣trM∣=ℏn, and (4.2.25) gives ℏ2n2≤n∥M∥F2\hbar^{2}n^{2}\le n\norm{M}_{F}^{2}ℏ2n2≤n∥M∥F2​, that is

  ∥[x^,p^]−iℏI^∥F  ≥  ℏn  =  ∥iℏI^∥F   \boxed{\;\norm{\big[\hat x,\hat p\big]-\ii\hbar\hat I}_{F} \;\ge\; \hbar\sqrt{n} \;=\; \norm{\ii\hbar\hat I}_{F}\;} ​[x^,p^​]−iℏI^​F​≥ℏn​=​iℏI^​F​​ (4.2.26)

for every pair of n×nn\times nn×n matrices and every nnn. Read the right-hand equality. The error is at least as large as the thing being reproduced. In relative terms the miss is at least 100%100\%100%, at every size, so a finite matrix pair cannot get the canonical commutator even half right.

Verified numerically, and the bound is attained. Minimising ∥[x^,p^]−iℏI^∥F/∥iℏI^∥F\norm{[\hat x,\hat p]-\ii\hbar\hat I}_{F}/\norm{\ii\hbar\hat I}_{F}​[x^,p^​]−iℏI^​F​/​iℏI^​F​ directly over all complex n×nn\times nn×n pairs by Nelder–Mead from twelve random starts bottoms out at 1.0000001.0000001.000000 for n=2,3,4,5n=2,3,4,5n=2,3,4,5, so the bound is right and it is attained. Problem 3 identifies the equality case, and it is worth having in advance. Equality needs MMM parallel to I^\hat II^, which forces [x^,p^]=0[\hat x,\hat p]=0[x^,p^​]=0. So the best a finite-dimensional model can do is to commute, that is to reproduce none of the relation at all, and every pair that makes the commutator non-zero does strictly worse. For the natural truncation x^=diag⁡(0,1,…,n−1)\hat x=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,\dots,n-1)x^=diag(0,1,…,n−1) with a nearest-neighbour p^\hat pp^​, the trace of the commutator is 000 to machine precision at n=4,16,64n=4,16,64n=4,16,64 and 256256256, exactly as (4.2.23) requires.

8.4 · Why spin is not a counterexample, and what has to happen next

Here is the objection to raise. Chapter 4.8 will describe electron spin with 2×22\times22×2 matrices, and that is finite-dimensional. It is, and no contradiction arises, because a spin has no position operator. The three spin components satisfy [S^i,S^j]=iℏϵijkS^k[\hat S_{i},\hat S_{j}]=\ii\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}\hat S_{k}[S^i​,S^j​]=iℏϵijk​S^k​, whose right-hand side is not a multiple of the identity. Its trace therefore can vanish, and does, since each S^k\hat S_{k}S^k​ is traceless. Section 8.2 rules out finite dimensions only for a system carrying a canonically conjugate pair. That it rules them out so cleanly while leaving spin alone is a check on the argument rather than a limitation of it.

What §8.2 forces, then, is this. The space of states for a particle has to be infinite-dimensional, and every theorem quoted in this chapter was proved in Chapter 0.5 in finite dimensions. Chapter 0.5 was explicit about the four places its proofs used that hypothesis, naming them as "in the induction, in rank–nullity, in the interchange of sums, in the claim that an injective map is surjective", and it said the bill would come due. It comes due in two instalments, and the division is worth stating precisely rather than gesturing at:

  • Chapter 4.3 builds the space. The Riemann integral is discarded and rebuilt as the Lebesgue integral. That is what makes L2L^{2}L2 complete, so that a limit of states is a state, and what makes the Fourier modes genuinely an orthonormal basis rather than an assumption. Everything in §§1–3 of this chapter that used "an orthonormal basis exists" is on credit until then.
  • Chapter 4.4 builds the operators on it. Unbounded operators, domains, the difference between symmetric and self-adjoint that P2's box already warned about, spectra with no eigenvectors, the spectral theorem in the form that survives, and the meaning of ∣x⟩\ket x∣x⟩ and ∣p⟩\ket p∣p⟩. Everything in §§4–7 that used "the spectral theorem" is on credit until then.

That two-chapter shape is not new. Chapter 0.4 built the space and Chapter 0.5 built the operators on it. Chapter 4.3 builds the space and Chapter 4.4 builds the operators on it, in the same order and for the same reason.

In plain terms 4.2.8

Position and momentum need a relation to each other, and the classical theory supplies one already: the bracket that measured how a quantity changes under the flow another one generates gave a particular answer for those two. The assertion here is that the same relation holds with the bracket replaced by the failure of two maps to commute, times a constant. That is a real assumption, and whether it can be extended to every quantity at once is a question with a sharp and negative answer several chapters ahead.

What the assertion costs is immediate and enormous, and the argument is three lines long. Adding up the diagonal entries of a product does not care about the order of multiplication, so the diagonal sum of the failure-to-commute is zero for any two square arrays whatever. The relation demands that it equal a fixed non-zero number on every diagonal entry, whose sum is therefore not zero. No finite list of numbers can do this. Not approximately either: the best possible attempt at any size misses by as much as the target itself.

So the space cannot be finite-dimensional, and this is settled before any physics is done. Two chapters of mathematics follow, and they were not chosen for thoroughness. They were forced here.

9 · Two systems: the tensor product

Announce the destination. Everything so far has described one system. Two systems require a rule for combining their state spaces, and there are only two candidates: the dimensions add, or the dimensions multiply. We build the object in which they multiply out of Chapter 0.4's basis and dimension, and it turns out to be a basis of pairs and nothing more. We postulate that it is the right one, and then we count. The counting is what makes entanglement a fact about arithmetic rather than a mystery, and it is the whole of what Chapter 4.11 needs from this chapter.

9.1 · A basis of pairs

Let system AAA have state space VVV with orthonormal basis {∣a1⟩,…,∣am⟩}\{\ket{a_{1}},\dots,\ket{a_{m}}\}{∣a1​⟩,…,∣am​⟩} and system BBB have WWW with {∣b1⟩,…,∣bn⟩}\{\ket{b_{1}},\dots,\ket{b_{n}}\}{∣b1​⟩,…,∣bn​⟩}. Whatever the joint space is, it must contain a state for each way of specifying both systems separately: AAA in ∣ai⟩\ket{a_{i}}∣ai​⟩ and BBB in ∣bj⟩\ket{b_{j}}∣bj​⟩. Write that state ∣ai⟩⊗∣bj⟩\ket{a_{i}}\otimes\ket{b_{j}}∣ai​⟩⊗∣bj​⟩, abbreviated ∣aibj⟩\ket{a_{i}b_{j}}∣ai​bj​⟩, and there are mnmnmn such pairs.

Now use P1. If those mnmnmn states are all possible states of the pair, then by the superposition principle so is every complex combination of them, and the joint space contains their span. Declare them to be an orthonormal basis of that span. That declaration is the definition of the tensor product V⊗WV\otimes WV⊗W, and by Chapter 0.4 §2.2's definition of dimension it gives

dim⁡(V⊗W)  =  (dim⁡V)(dim⁡W)  =  mn. \dim\big(V\otimes W\big) \;=\; \big(\dim V\big)\big(\dim W\big) \;=\; mn. dim(V⊗W)=(dimV)(dimW)=mn. (4.2.27)

The inner product comes with it, and nothing new has to be chosen. Declare ⟨aibj ∣ akbl⟩=δikδjl\avg{a_{i}b_{j}\,|\,a_{k}b_{l}}=\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}⟨ai​bj​∣ak​bl​⟩=δik​δjl​ on the basis and extend by conjugate-linearity in the first slot and linearity in the second, which is Chapter 0.5 §1's construction unchanged. For a general pair of states ∣ϕ⟩=∑iϕi∣ai⟩\ket\phi=\sum_{i}\phi_{i}\ket{a_{i}}∣ϕ⟩=∑i​ϕi​∣ai​⟩ and ∣χ⟩=∑jχj∣bj⟩\ket\chi=\sum_{j}\chi_{j}\ket{b_{j}}∣χ⟩=∑j​χj​∣bj​⟩ this gives

∣ϕ⟩⊗∣χ⟩  =  ∑i,jϕiχj ∣aibj⟩,⟨ϕ⊗χ ∣ ϕ′⊗χ′⟩  =  ⟨ϕ∣ϕ′⟩⟨χ∣χ′⟩, \ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{\chi} \;=\; \sum_{i,j}\phi_{i}\chi_{j}\,\ket{a_{i}b_{j}}, \qquad \avg{\phi\otimes\chi\,|\,\phi'\otimes\chi'} \;=\; \avg{\phi|\phi'}\avg{\chi|\chi'}, ∣ϕ⟩⊗∣χ⟩=i,j∑​ϕi​χj​∣ai​bj​⟩,⟨ϕ⊗χ∣ϕ′⊗χ′⟩=⟨ϕ∣ϕ′⟩⟨χ∣χ′⟩, (4.2.28)

the second identity following by expanding both sides on the basis and collapsing with the deltas. Amplitudes for independent systems multiply, which is what they had better do.

⚑ P7 — the composition postulate

Asserted. The state space of a system composed of two parts is the tensor product of the parts' state spaces, so its dimension is the product of theirs. Observables belonging to part AAA alone act as A^⊗I^\hat A\otimes\hat IA^⊗I^, and any two such observables commute with any two belonging to BBB alone.

Not derived. There is a competing rule, which says that describing two systems means listing two descriptions, so that the dimensions add. That is what classical mechanics does with configuration spaces, and nothing in P1 to P6 rules it out. Which one nature uses is a physical question, and its answer is the source of every effect in Chapter 4.11.

What is not being claimed. Nothing here says a state of the whole is built from states of the parts, and §9.2 shows almost none of them are. Nothing here handles identical parts either, where a further restriction applies. That restriction is P8, the symmetrisation postulate, and it is stated in Chapter 4.11 §3.

9.2 · Entanglement, as a dimension count

Ask how many of the mnmnmn dimensions are reached by states of the form ∣ϕ⟩⊗∣χ⟩\ket\phi\otimes\ket\chi∣ϕ⟩⊗∣χ⟩. Count parameters. Choosing ∣ϕ⟩\ket\phi∣ϕ⟩ takes mmm complex numbers and ∣χ⟩\ket\chi∣χ⟩ takes nnn, but rescaling ∣ϕ⟩\ket\phi∣ϕ⟩ by ccc and ∣χ⟩\ket\chi∣χ⟩ by 1/c1/c1/c gives the same product, so one complex parameter is shared. The set of product vectors therefore has complex dimension m+n−1m+n-1m+n−1, inside a space of complex dimension mnmnmn. For two two-level systems that is 333 inside 444. For two ten-level systems it is 191919 inside 100100100.

So almost every state of a composite system is not a pair of states of its parts. Such states are called entangled, and the word names a counting fact rather than an influence: the joint space has more directions in it than the product construction reaches.

One explicit case, checkable by hand in three lines. Take two two-level systems and the state 12(∣00⟩+∣11⟩)\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(\ket{00}+\ket{11}\big)2​1​(∣00⟩+∣11⟩). If it were (a∣0⟩+b∣1⟩)⊗(c∣0⟩+d∣1⟩)=ac∣00⟩+ad∣01⟩+bc∣10⟩+bd∣11⟩\big(a\ket0+b\ket1\big)\otimes\big(c\ket0+d\ket1\big)=ac\ket{00}+ad\ket{01}+bc\ket{10}+bd\ket{11}(a∣0⟩+b∣1⟩)⊗(c∣0⟩+d∣1⟩)=ac∣00⟩+ad∣01⟩+bc∣10⟩+bd∣11⟩, then matching coefficients requires

ac=12,bd=12,ad=0,bc=0. ac=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, \qquad bd=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, \qquad ad=0, \qquad bc=0. ac=2​1​,bd=2​1​,ad=0,bc=0. (4.2.29)

From ad=0ad=0ad=0 either a=0a=0a=0, which contradicts ac=1/2ac=1/\sqrt2ac=1/2​, or d=0d=0d=0, which contradicts bd=1/2bd=1/\sqrt2bd=1/2​. No solution exists. The state assigns no state at all to either half on its own, and the question "what is the first system's state?" has no answer of the kind P1 provides. That is why Chapter 4.11 has to build a different object, the density operator, to answer it.

9.3 · The size of the space, with a number

Iterating (4.2.27) over NNN two-level systems gives a state space of dimension 2N2^{N}2N, so specifying a general state takes 2N2^{N}2N complex amplitudes, while specifying a state of each system separately takes 2N2N2N real angles by (4.2.5). At N=300N=300N=300:

2300  =  2.04×1090amplitudes,against600angles. 2^{300} \;=\; 2.04\times10^{90} \quad\text{amplitudes}, \qquad\text{against}\qquad 600 \quad\text{angles}. 2300=2.04×1090amplitudes,against600angles. (4.2.30)

The observable universe contains of order 108010^{80}1080 atoms. Three hundred two-level systems means three hundred atoms, which is a small molecule. They have more amplitudes in their joint description than there are atoms available to record them, and the excess is entirely the gap between mnmnmn and m+n−1m+n-1m+n−1, compounded three hundred times. That gap is what makes simulating quantum systems on ordinary computers hard, what makes building quantum ones interesting, and what Chapter 4.11 measures with Bell's inequality. It follows from P7 and nothing else.

In plain terms 4.2.9

Put two systems side by side and ask what describes the pair. The answer is the one place where quantum mechanics departs from ordinary intuition by an amount that can be written as a number. Classically, describing two things means describing each and listing both, so the descriptions add. Here a basis for the pair is a list of pairs of basis states, one drawn from each, so the dimensions multiply.

That difference is entirely responsible for the phenomenon everyone finds strange. States describing each system separately and then pairing them do exist, but they form a vanishingly thin subset — counted properly, of dimension roughly the sum where the whole space has dimension the product. Almost every state of the pair is therefore not of that form, which means it assigns no state at all to either half on its own. A concrete two-by-two example can be checked by hand in three lines: four conditions on four numbers, and no solution.

The practical scale of this is worth a number. Three hundred two-state systems require more amplitudes to specify than there are atoms in the observable universe, while a description of each one separately needs six hundred angles. That gap is where the interest in building such machines comes from, and the last chapter of this part is about what fills it.

10 · Three two-state systems, in full

Announce the destination. Chapter 0.5's Worked example 1 diagonalised one 2×22\times22×2 Hermitian matrix completely and then said what it was: "It is the ammonia molecule… it is neutrino oscillation… it is the qubit. Chapter 4.2 will do all three, and the linear algebra will already be finished." Here it is done. We solve the matrix once with §7's evolution operator, and obtain a single formula. Then we read that formula three times, in three sets of units: picoseconds, kilometres, nanoseconds. The linear algebra takes half a page because it was finished nine chapters ago. The rest is identification and arithmetic.

10.1 · One matrix, solved once

Two states, called ∣1⟩\ket1∣1⟩ and ∣2⟩\ket2∣2⟩, whatever they turn out to be physically. The most general Hermitian operator on their span has four real parameters. One of them, the phase of the off-diagonal entry, can be absorbed into the definition of ∣2⟩\ket2∣2⟩, so take it real. Write the remaining three as a mean, a difference and a coupling:

H^  =  (Eˉ+δΔΔEˉ−δ),Eˉ, δ, Δ∈R,Δ>0. \hat H \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \bar E+\delta & \Delta\\[2pt] \Delta & \bar E-\delta\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \bar E,\ \delta,\ \Delta\in\R,\quad \Delta\gt0. H^=(Eˉ+δΔ​ΔEˉ−δ​),Eˉ, δ, Δ∈R,Δ>0. (4.2.31)

Chapter 0.5's Worked example 1 is the case δ=0\delta=0δ=0. The eigenvalues come from the characteristic polynomial, (Eˉ+δ−λ)(Eˉ−δ−λ)−Δ2=0(\bar E+\delta-\lambda)(\bar E-\delta-\lambda)-\Delta^{2}=0(Eˉ+δ−λ)(Eˉ−δ−λ)−Δ2=0, giving

E±  =  Eˉ±R,R  ≡  δ2+Δ2,ΔE  ≡  E+−E−  =  2R. E_{\pm} \;=\; \bar E \pm R, \qquad R \;\equiv\; \sqrt{\delta^{2}+\Delta^{2}}, \qquad \Delta E \;\equiv\; E_{+}-E_{-} \;=\; 2R. E±​=Eˉ±R,R≡δ2+Δ2​,ΔE≡E+​−E−​=2R. (4.2.32)

Real, as Chapter 0.5 §6.1 requires, and the level splitting is ΔE=2R\Delta E=2RΔE=2R. Notice the shape. The coupling Δ\DeltaΔ pushes the two levels apart whatever the diagonal difference is, and the splitting is never smaller than 2Δ2\Delta2Δ. Two levels that would cross as δ\deltaδ passes through zero instead approach to 2Δ2\Delta2Δ and separate again. That is an avoided crossing, and the phenomenon is entirely (4.2.32).

Define the mixing angle θ\thetaθ by

cos⁡2θ  =  δR,sin⁡2θ  =  ΔR,equivalentlytan⁡2θ=Δδ, \cos2\theta \;=\; \frac{\delta}{R}, \qquad \sin2\theta \;=\; \frac{\Delta}{R}, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \tan2\theta=\frac{\Delta}{\delta}, cos2θ=Rδ​,sin2θ=RΔ​,equivalentlytan2θ=δΔ​, (4.2.33)

which is legitimate because cos⁡22θ+sin⁡22θ=(δ2+Δ2)/R2=1\cos^{2}2\theta+\sin^{2}2\theta=(\delta^{2}+\Delta^{2})/R^{2}=1cos22θ+sin22θ=(δ2+Δ2)/R2=1. Then the normalised eigenvectors are

∣+⟩  =  cos⁡θ ∣1⟩+sin⁡θ ∣2⟩,∣−⟩  =  −sin⁡θ ∣1⟩+cos⁡θ ∣2⟩, \ket{+} \;=\; \cos\theta\,\ket1+\sin\theta\,\ket2, \qquad \ket{-} \;=\; -\sin\theta\,\ket1+\cos\theta\,\ket2, ∣+⟩=cosθ∣1⟩+sinθ∣2⟩,∣−⟩=−sinθ∣1⟩+cosθ∣2⟩, (4.2.34)

orthogonal by inspection, as Chapter 0.5 §6.2 guarantees without being consulted. The grind box verifies them and runs §7's evolution operator on the state that starts as ∣1⟩\ket1∣1⟩. The result is one formula, and it is the whole of this section:

  P1→2(t)  =  sin⁡22θ  sin⁡2 ⁣(ΔE t2ℏ)  =  Δ2δ2+Δ2 sin⁡2 ⁣(δ2+Δ2  tℏ)   \boxed{\;P_{1\to2}(t) \;=\; \sin^{2}2\theta\;\sin^{2}\!\left(\frac{\Delta E\,t}{2\hbar}\right) \;=\; \frac{\Delta^{2}}{\delta^{2}+\Delta^{2}}\,\sin^{2}\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{\delta^{2}+\Delta^{2}}\;t}{\hbar}\right)\;} P1→2​(t)=sin22θsin2(2ℏΔEt​)=δ2+Δ2Δ2​sin2(ℏδ2+Δ2​t​)​ (4.2.35)

with P1→1=1−P1→2P_{1\to1}=1-P_{1\to2}P1→1​=1−P1→2​ exactly. Four features are worth naming before the physics starts, because each is one of this chapter's postulates doing visible work.

The mean energy Eˉ\bar EEˉ does not appear. It cancelled, because it contributes an overall factor e−iEˉt/ℏ\ee^{-\ii\bar Et/\hbar}e−iEˉt/ℏ to the state. That is a global phase, which P1 says is not there. Only energy differences are observable, and that is P1 rather than a separate principle.

The oscillation never stops and never damps. By §7's familiar box, the eigenvalues of the generator are purely imaginary, so nothing decays. A classical two-state rate process would relax to fifty-fifty and stay there.

Depth and speed move in opposite directions. Increasing the detuning δ\deltaδ at fixed coupling makes sin⁡22θ\sin^{2}2\thetasin22θ smaller, which is a shallower oscillation, and RRR larger, which is a faster one.

And at short times the two effects cancel exactly. Expanding (4.2.35) for small ttt, the sin⁡2\sin^{2}sin2 contributes R2t2/ℏ2R^{2}t^{2}/\hbar^{2}R2t2/ℏ2 and the prefactor contributes Δ2/R2\Delta^{2}/R^{2}Δ2/R2, so

and the leading term does not contain δ\deltaδ at all. However far off resonance the system is driven, the transition probability leaves zero along the same parabola. Detuning changes when the curve turns over, not how fast it starts. That is the seed of the transition-rate formula Chapter 4.10 derives, and the figure below makes it visible.

Ammonia. The inversion line of NH3\mathrm{NH}_{3}NH3​ in the (J,K)=(3,3)(J,K)=(3,3)(J,K)=(3,3) rotational state is at ν0=23.8701 GHz\nu_{0}=23.8701\ \mathrm{GHz}ν0​=23.8701 GHz, which is the line the first maser ran on in 1954. The corresponding splitting for the non-rotating molecule is 0.7934 cm−1=23.7855 GHz0.7934\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}=23.7855\ \mathrm{GHz}0.7934 cm−1=23.7855 GHz. The barrier to inversion is about 2020 cm−12020\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}2020 cm−1.

Neutrinos. Δm322=2.45×10−3 eV2\Delta m^{2}_{32}=2.45\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV^{2}}Δm322​=2.45×10−3 eV2 with sin⁡22θ23\sin^{2}2\theta_{23}sin22θ23​ consistent with 111. Then sin⁡22θ13=0.085\sin^{2}2\theta_{13}=0.085sin22θ13​=0.085 with Δm312=2.5×10−3 eV2\Delta m^{2}_{31}=2.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV^{2}}Δm312​=2.5×10−3 eV2. Baselines and energies as quoted per experiment.

Qubit. A superconducting two-level circuit with level splitting ω0/2π=5 GHz\omega_{0}/2\pi=5\ \mathrm{GHz}ω0​/2π=5 GHz, driven at a Rabi frequency ΩR/2π=25 MHz\Omega_{R}/2\pi=25\ \mathrm{MHz}ΩR​/2π=25 MHz. These are representative numbers for a transmon, chosen because they are round.

The two-state description itself is a model in every case.

  • Ammonia is a molecule with many vibrational and rotational levels, and the two-state treatment is the restriction to the lowest inversion doublet.
  • The neutrino has three flavours, and the two-flavour treatment is exact only when one mass splitting dominates.
  • The qubit is a weakly anharmonic ladder truncated to its bottom two rungs.

Each restriction is a good approximation for the reason its own field gives, and none of them is being derived here.

10.2 · The ammonia molecule

Ammonia is a nitrogen atom and three hydrogens arranged as a shallow pyramid. The nitrogen can sit above the plane of the hydrogens or below it, and these two arrangements are mirror images with identical energy. Call them ∣L⟩\ket L∣L⟩ and ∣R⟩\ket R∣R⟩. Two facts fix (4.2.31) completely.

The detuning is zero, by symmetry. Reflecting the molecule exchanges ∣L⟩\ket L∣L⟩ and ∣R⟩\ket R∣R⟩ and changes no energy, so the two diagonal entries of H^\hat HH^ are equal and δ=0\delta=0δ=0. This is not an approximation or a convenient choice. It is a symmetry of the Coulomb interaction between the same four nuclei and the same ten electrons. Hence by (4.2.33), θ=π/4\theta=\pi/4θ=π/4 and sin⁡22θ=1\sin^{2}2\theta=1sin22θ=1, and the oscillation goes all the way from one configuration to the other and back.

The coupling is not zero. Classically the nitrogen cannot get from one side to the other, because passing through the plane of the hydrogens costs about 2020 cm−12020\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}2020 cm−1, which is 0.2504 eV0.2504\ \mathrm{eV}0.2504 eV, far more than the molecule has. The off-diagonal entry Δ\DeltaΔ of a Hermitian operator connecting ∣L⟩\ket L∣L⟩ and ∣R⟩\ket R∣R⟩ is under no such prohibition. Nothing in P1 to P5 requires a state to get from one place to another through the intervening places, and Chapter 4.6 computes Δ\DeltaΔ for a barrier. Here it is read off a measurement.

So the energy eigenstates are the symmetric and antisymmetric combinations, ∣±⟩=(∣L⟩±∣R⟩)/2\ket\pm=(\ket L\pm\ket R)/\sqrt2∣±⟩=(∣L⟩±∣R⟩)/2​, split by ΔE=2Δ\Delta E=2\DeltaΔE=2Δ, and

PL→R(t)  =  sin⁡2 ⁣(ΔE t2ℏ)  =  sin⁡2(πν0t),ΔE  =  hν0. P_{L\to R}(t) \;=\; \sin^{2}\!\left(\frac{\Delta E\,t}{2\hbar}\right) \;=\; \sin^{2}\big(\pi\nu_{0}t\big), \qquad \Delta E \;=\; h\nu_{0}. PL→R​(t)=sin2(2ℏΔEt​)=sin2(πν0​t),ΔE=hν0​. (4.2.37)

We want a number out of that rather than a shape, so put the measured ν0=23.8701 GHz\nu_{0}=23.8701\ \mathrm{GHz}ν0​=23.8701 GHz into it. The splitting is

ΔE  =  hν0  =  6.62607015×10−34×2.38701×1010=  1.58165×10−23 J  =  98.72 μeV, \begin{aligned} \Delta E \;=\; h\nu_{0} \;&=\; 6.62607015\times10^{-34}\times2.38701\times10^{10}\\[3pt] &=\; 1.58165\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J} \;=\; 98.72\ \mu\mathrm{eV}, \end{aligned} ΔE=hν0​​=6.62607015×10−34×2.38701×1010=1.58165×10−23 J=98.72 μeV,​ (4.2.38)

and the time for the molecule to turn itself inside out and back is 1/ν0=41.89 ps1/\nu_{0}=41.89\ \mathrm{ps}1/ν0​=41.89 ps, with the halfway point, nitrogen fully on the other side, at 20.95 ps20.95\ \mathrm{ps}20.95 ps. Three consequences follow, and each of them is a postulate of this chapter made visible.

A molecule in its ground state has no shape. The stationary states are ∣±⟩\ket\pm∣±⟩, not ∣L⟩\ket L∣L⟩ or ∣R⟩\ket R∣R⟩. A state of definite shape is a superposition of the two energy levels, and therefore not stationary. This is §4.3 in the most concrete form available. Shape and energy are represented by operators that do not commute, so there is no state with both sharp, and the molecule in its lowest energy level is not in either configuration.

The splitting is tiny because the barrier is large. The ratio of barrier to splitting is 0.2504 eV/98.72 μeV=25360.2504\ \mathrm{eV}/98.72\ \mu\mathrm{eV}=25360.2504 eV/98.72 μeV=2536. That the coupling is suppressed by three orders of magnitude rather than being zero is the quantitative content of tunnelling, and Chapter 4.7's WKB approximation computes the suppression as an exponential in the barrier's width and height.

The frequency lands in the microwave band, which is why the maser came first. The wavelength is c/ν0=1.2559 cmc/\nu_{0}=1.2559\ \mathrm{cm}c/ν0​=1.2559 cm. Chapter 4.1's Worked example 3 derived the ratio of stimulated to spontaneous emission for an atom in thermal radiation as 1/(ehν/kBT−1)1/(\ee^{h\nu/k_{B}T}-1)1/(ehν/kB​T−1). At 23.8701 GHz23.8701\ \mathrm{GHz}23.8701 GHz and 300 K300\ \mathrm{K}300 K, hν/kBT=3.819×10−3h\nu/k_{B}T=3.819\times10^{-3}hν/kB​T=3.819×10−3, and the ratio is

RstimRspont  =  1e0.003819−1  =  261.4, \frac{R^{\text{stim}}}{R^{\text{spont}}} \;=\; \frac{1}{\ee^{0.003819}-1} \;=\; 261.4, RspontRstim​=e0.003819−11​=261.4, (4.2.39)

so stimulated emission beats spontaneous emission by a factor of 260260260 at room temperature at this frequency, against 10−3310^{-33}10−33 for an optical transition. Now sort the two energy eigenstates with an inhomogeneous electric field, which works because ∣±⟩\ket\pm∣±⟩ have opposite parity and so respond oppositely. Feed the upper one into a cavity tuned to 1.26 cm1.26\ \mathrm{cm}1.26 cm, and the third process Einstein was forced to invent in Chapter 4.1 §4.5 amplifies. That is the ammonia maser, built in 1954, and every number in its design is in this paragraph.

10.3 · Neutrino oscillation

The same matrix, and the identification is where all the work is. A neutrino is produced by a weak interaction in a definite flavour, with a muon or with an electron, and it is detected the same way. But flavour is not what propagation cares about. Propagation is generated by H^\hat HH^, whose eigenstates are the states of definite mass.

Call the flavour states ∣νμ⟩\ket{\nu_{\mu}}∣νμ​⟩ and ∣ντ⟩\ket{\nu_{\tau}}∣ντ​⟩, and the mass states ∣ν1⟩\ket{\nu_{1}}∣ν1​⟩ and ∣ν2⟩\ket{\nu_{2}}∣ν2​⟩. The assertion tested by every oscillation experiment is that these are two different orthonormal bases of the same two-dimensional space, related by (4.2.34) for some angle θ\thetaθ. Nothing about that is unusual. It is Chapter 0.4's change of basis, and §4.3 of this chapter says the two observables do not commute.

Now the energies, and this is the one step needing Part II. A neutrino of definite mass mim_{i}mi​ and momentum ppp has, by Chapter 2.5 §4.3, energy Ei=p2c2+mi2c4E_{i}=\sqrt{p^{2}c^{2}+m_{i}^{2}c^{4}}Ei​=p2c2+mi2​c4​. Neutrinos in these experiments carry energies in the MeV to GeV range, while their masses are below an electronvolt, so mic2≪pcm_{i}c^{2}\ll pcmi​c2≪pc and the square root can be expanded. We want the difference of two nearly equal energies, and the leading terms will cancel, which is exactly why expanding is the right move:

Ei  =  pc1+mi2c2p2  =  pc  +  mi2c32p  +  O ⁣(m4c5p3), E_{i} \;=\; pc\sqrt{1+\frac{m_{i}^{2}c^{2}}{p^{2}}} \;=\; pc \;+\; \frac{m_{i}^{2}c^{3}}{2p} \;+\; O\!\left(\frac{m^{4}c^{5}}{p^{3}}\right), Ei​=pc1+p2mi2​c2​​=pc+2pmi2​c3​+O(p3m4c5​), (4.2.40)

using 1+u=1+u/2+O(u2)\sqrt{1+u}=1+u/2+O(u^{2})1+u​=1+u/2+O(u2) from Chapter 0.3. The common pcpcpc cancels in the difference, and with E≈pcE\approx pcE≈pc for the beam energy,

That is the level splitting in (4.2.35). One more identification is needed. A neutrino travels at essentially ccc, so the proper substitution for the elapsed time is t=L/ct=L/ct=L/c, where LLL is the distance from source to detector. That distance is the quantity an experiment actually controls. Substituting both into (4.2.35):

Δm2c4L4ℏcE  =  Δm2×L×1034×1.973269804×10−7×E×109  =  1.26693 Δm2 LE, \frac{\Delta m^{2}c^{4}L}{4\hbar cE} \;=\; \frac{\Delta m^{2}\times L\times10^{3}}{4\times1.973269804\times10^{-7}\times E\times10^{9}} \;=\; 1.26693\,\frac{\Delta m^{2}\,L}{E}, 4ℏcEΔm2c4L​=4×1.973269804×10−7×E×109Δm2×L×103​=1.26693EΔm2L​, (4.2.43)

The same formula with a small mixing angle gives the other kind of experiment. At the Daya Bay reactor, electron antineutrinos of about 4 MeV4\ \mathrm{MeV}4 MeV are counted at L=1.65 kmL=1.65\ \mathrm{km}L=1.65 km. One honesty note about the derivation. Treating the two mass states as plane waves with a common momentum, and setting t=L/ct=L/ct=L/c, is a shortcut. A neutrino is produced as a localised wave packet, the two mass components travel at slightly different speeds, and the careful treatment follows the packets and asks when they still overlap at the detector. It gives (4.2.42) in every regime these experiments operate in, and the corrections are suppressed by the ratio of the packet width to LoscL_{\text{osc}}Losc​. The shortcut is standard, and it is a shortcut. The machinery to do it properly is Chapter 4.5's wave packets.

10.4 · The qubit

The third reading inverts the relationship between the formula and the apparatus. In ammonia the parameters are whatever chemistry supplies. In a neutrino they are whatever the mass matrix supplies. In an engineered two-level system both are set by the designer, and (4.2.35) becomes a specification rather than a prediction.

Take a superconducting circuit with two levels split by ℏω0\hbar\omega_{0}ℏω0​, with ω0/2π=5 GHz\omega_{0}/2\pi=5\ \mathrm{GHz}ω0​/2π=5 GHz. That is a splitting of 20.68 μeV20.68\ \mu\mathrm{eV}20.68 μeV, which is twelve times kBT=1.72 μeVk_{B}T=1.72\ \mu\mathrm{eV}kB​T=1.72 μeV at the 20 mK20\ \mathrm{mK}20 mK such circuits run at. So Chapter 0.6's Boltzmann factor e−ΔE/kBT=6×10−6\ee^{-\Delta E/k_{B}T}=6\times10^{-6}e−ΔE/kB​T=6×10−6 leaves the system in its lower level rather than thermally stirred.

Now drive it with a microwave field at exactly ω0\omega_{0}ω0​. Chapter 4.10 shows that in a frame rotating with the drive the problem becomes (4.2.31) with δ=0\delta=0δ=0 and Δ=ℏΩR/2\Delta=\hbar\Omega_{R}/2Δ=ℏΩR​/2, where ΩR\Omega_{R}ΩR​ is proportional to the drive amplitude. That reduction is Chapter 4.10's and is not derived here. With it granted, (4.2.35) reads

P0→1(t)  =  sin⁡2 ⁣(ΩRt2), P_{0\to1}(t) \;=\; \sin^{2}\!\left(\frac{\Omega_{R}t}{2}\right), P0→1​(t)=sin2(2ΩR​t​), (4.2.46)

the Rabi formula. With ΩR/2π=25 MHz\Omega_{R}/2\pi=25\ \mathrm{MHz}ΩR​/2π=25 MHz the full period is 40 ns40\ \mathrm{ns}40 ns, so a pulse lasting

tπ  =  πΩR  =  12×25 MHz  =  20 ns t_{\pi} \;=\; \frac{\pi}{\Omega_{R}} \;=\; \frac{1}{2\times25\ \mathrm{MHz}} \;=\; 20\ \mathrm{ns} tπ​=ΩR​π​=2×25 MHz1​=20 ns (4.2.47)

takes ∣0⟩\ket0∣0⟩ to ∣1⟩\ket1∣1⟩ with probability 111. That is a NOT gate, performed by leaving the drive on for exactly half an oscillation. Half that, 10 ns10\ \mathrm{ns}10 ns, gives probability 12\half21​ and produces the operator whose square is NOT. Worked example 3 builds it and shows that no classical stochastic process has such a square root. Detuning the drive off resonance is δ≠0\delta\neq0δ=0, and (4.2.35) says the gate then fails to reach probability 111 no matter how long it is left on, with the shortfall 1−sin⁡22θ=δ2/(δ2+Δ2)1-\sin^{2}2\theta=\delta^{2}/(\delta^{2}+\Delta^{2})1−sin22θ=δ2/(δ2+Δ2). That is where the tolerance on a control line comes from.

10.5 · One computed evolution, read in three sets of units

The figure below integrates (4.2.18) numerically for (4.2.31) and plots what comes out. Nothing in it uses (4.2.35). The closed form appears only in the readout, as the thing being checked against. Two of the readouts are the numerical confirmation this chapter owes.

In plain terms 4.2.10

The point of this section is that there is one calculation, and it is finished. Take two states of nearly the same energy with something connecting them, which is the smallest interesting arrangement there is, and solve it once. What comes out is a single expression: the chance of finding the system in the other state swings back and forth forever, at a rate set by the separation of the two energy levels, with a depth set by how evenly the connection mixes them.

Now read the answer three times. In a molecule of ammonia the two states are the nitrogen atom sitting on either side of its three hydrogens, the connection is its ability to pass through them, and the swing takes forty-two trillionths of a second — which corresponds to a microwave line that was used to build the first device of its kind. In a neutrino the two states are the two identities it can be detected with, the connection is the mismatch between those and the two definite masses, and the swing takes six hundred kilometres of flight. In an engineered two-level circuit both numbers are chosen by the designer, and half a swing at twenty nanoseconds is what turns one state into the other.

Three subjects, three sets of units, one matrix. That is what the chapter has been claiming.

11 · Worked examples

Worked example 1 — three magnets in a row, and what P4 does that P3 cannot

A beam of spin-12\half21​ particles is prepared with a definite value of S^z\hat S_{z}S^z​, passed through a second apparatus measuring S^x\hat S_{x}S^x​, and then through a third measuring S^z\hat S_{z}S^z​ again. Using only P3 and P4: (a) compute the probability of the third magnet reporting spin-down. (b) Compute the same probability with the middle magnet removed. (c) Compute it with the middle magnet present but not read, so that the two xxx-paths are recombined coherently. (d) Say which postulate each answer used, and what the comparison establishes.

Set up the two-dimensional space with ∣z+⟩,∣z−⟩\ket{z{+}},\ket{z{-}}∣z+⟩,∣z−⟩ an orthonormal basis. The observable S^x\hat S_{x}S^x​ has, by Chapter 0.5's Worked example 1 with E0=0E_{0}=0E0​=0, the eigenstates

∣x±⟩  =  12(∣z+⟩±∣z−⟩), \ket{x{\pm}} \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(\ket{z{+}}\pm\ket{z{-}}\big), ∣x±⟩=2​1​(∣z+⟩±∣z−⟩),

which are orthogonal, as §4.1 requires without being asked. All four overlaps between the two bases have modulus 1/21/\sqrt21/2​.

(a) Measure, keep the +++ beam, measure again. Starting from ∣z+⟩\ket{z{+}}∣z+⟩, P3 gives Pr⁡(x+)=∣⟨x+∣z+⟩∣2=12\Pr(x{+})=\abs{\avg{x{+}|z{+}}}^{2}=\halfPr(x+)=∣⟨x+∣z+⟩∣2=21​, and P4 replaces the state by ∣x+⟩\ket{x{+}}∣x+⟩. Then P3 again: Pr⁡(z−)=∣⟨z−∣x+⟩∣2=12\Pr(z{-})=\abs{\avg{z{-}|x{+}}}^{2}=\halfPr(z−)=∣⟨z−∣x+⟩∣2=21​. The two are independent because P4 wiped out all memory of the first state, so

Pr⁡(z+→x+→z−)  =  12×12  =  14. \Pr(z{+}\to x{+}\to z{-}) \;=\; \tfrac12\times\tfrac12 \;=\; \tfrac14. Pr(z+→x+→z−)=21​×21​=41​.

(b) Middle magnet removed. Nothing happens between the two zzz measurements, so the state is still ∣z+⟩\ket{z{+}}∣z+⟩ and P3 gives Pr⁡(z−)=∣⟨z−∣z+⟩∣2=0\Pr(z{-})=\abs{\avg{z{-}|z{+}}}^{2}=0Pr(z−)=∣⟨z−∣z+⟩∣2=0, exactly. The two eigenstates of S^z\hat S_{z}S^z​ are orthogonal, and §4.1's second theorem says the confusion probability is zero rather than small.

(c) Middle magnet present, nothing read, beams recombined. Now no measurement occurred, so P4 does not apply and P3 is used once at the end. The state is unchanged and can be rewritten using the resolution of the identity in the xxx basis, which is Chapter 0.5 §2.3's ∑∣ei⟩⟨ei∣=I^\sum\ket{e_{i}}\bra{e_{i}}=\hat I∑∣ei​⟩⟨ei​∣=I^ inserted and nothing more:

⟨z−∣z+⟩=⟨z−∣I^∣z+⟩=⟨z−∣x+⟩⟨x+∣z+⟩⏟+12+⟨z−∣x−⟩⟨x−∣z+⟩⏟−12  =  0. \avg{z{-}|z{+}} = \avg{z{-}|\hat I|z{+}} = \underbrace{\avg{z{-}|x{+}}\avg{x{+}|z{+}}}_{+\frac12} + \underbrace{\avg{z{-}|x{-}}\avg{x{-}|z{+}}}_{-\frac12} \;=\; 0. ⟨z−∣z+⟩=⟨z−∣I^∣z+⟩=+21​⟨z−∣x+⟩⟨x+∣z+⟩​​+−21​⟨z−∣x−⟩⟨x−∣z+⟩​​=0.

The two amplitudes are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign, and they cancel exactly. So the answer is 000, agreeing with (b) as it must, since inserting I^\hat II^ changes nothing.

(d) What the three answers establish. Compare (a) with (c). The same apparatus is in the beam line in both, the same two paths are travelled, and the same final measurement is made. In (c) the two amplitudes are added and then squared, giving ∣12−12∣2=0\abs{\tfrac12-\tfrac12}^{2}=0​21​−21​​2=0. In (a) they are squared and then added, giving 14+14\tfrac14+\tfrac1441​+41​, of which one branch was kept, so 14\tfrac1441​. The only difference in the beam line is that in (a) the intermediate value was read. Keeping one branch afterwards is what turns the 12\tfrac1221​ into 14\tfrac1441​, and the reading is what destroyed the cancellation.

Certainty becomes a coin flip because somebody looked. That is P4 doing work that P3 alone cannot do. P3 assigns probabilities to the outcomes of a measurement, and it is P4 that destroys the coherence between the branches so that the third magnet sees no interference. It also shows why §6.2's familiar box insisted that conditioning is not the whole story. The classical law of total probability would give Pr⁡(z−)=∑kPr⁡(z−∣xk)Pr⁡(xk)=14+14=12\Pr(z{-})=\sum_{k}\Pr(z{-}\mid x_{k})\Pr(x_{k}) =\tfrac14+\tfrac14=\tfrac12Pr(z−)=∑k​Pr(z−∣xk​)Pr(xk​)=41​+41​=21​ whether anyone looked or not, and the measured answer without looking is 000.

Inside the +1+1+1 eigenspace of A^\hat AA^, the operator B^\hat BB^ has eigenvalue +1+1+1 on 12(1,1,0)\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1,0)2​1​(1,1,0) and −1-1−1 on (0,0,1)(0,0,1)(0,0,1), so it chooses the basis A^\hat AA^ could not. That is Chapter 0.5 §8.2's Step 4, in three dimensions. The joint labels are

(a,b)=(+1,+1) → 12(1,1,0),(+1,−1) → (0,0,1),(−1,+1) → 12(1,−1,0), \big(a,b\big) = (+1,+1)\ \to\ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1,0), \qquad (+1,-1)\ \to\ (0,0,1), \qquad (-1,+1)\ \to\ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,-1,0), (a,b)=(+1,+1) → 2​1​(1,1,0),(+1,−1) → (0,0,1),(−1,+1) → 2​1​(1,−1,0),

each one-dimensional, so {A^,B^}\{\hat A,\hat B\}{A^,B^} is a complete set of commuting observables and those pairs are the quantum numbers of §4.3. Measuring B^\hat BB^ on ∣ψ′⟩\ket{\psi'}∣ψ′⟩ gives Pr⁡(+1)=∣12(3+3)/34∣2=917\Pr(+1)=\abs{\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(3+3)/\sqrt{34}}^{2}=\tfrac{9}{17}Pr(+1)=​2​1​(3+3)/34​​2=179​ and Pr⁡(−1)=∣4/34∣2=817\Pr(-1)=\abs{4/\sqrt{34}}^{2}=\tfrac{8}{17}Pr(−1)=​4/34​​2=178​, summing to one, and after it the state carries a complete label.

Worked example 3 — the square root of NOT, and why no classical process has one

Section 10.4 said that half a Rabi period turns ∣0⟩\ket0∣0⟩ into ∣1⟩\ket1∣1⟩ with certainty, and that a quarter period produces an operator whose square is that gate. (a) Build the quarter-period operator from §7 and check it is unitary. (b) Square it. (c) Show that the classical analogue does not exist, meaning a two-state stochastic process whose square is a certain flip. (d) Say which postulate the difference belongs to.

(a) The resonant drive of §10.4 is (4.2.31) with δ=0\delta=0δ=0 and Eˉ=0\bar E=0Eˉ=0, so H^=Δσx\hat H=\Delta\sigma_{x}H^=Δσx​ and by (4.2.17) the evolution operator is U^(t)=e−iΔσxt/ℏ\hat U(t)=\ee^{-\ii\Delta\sigma_{x}t/\hbar}U^(t)=e−iΔσx​t/ℏ. Chapter 0.5's Worked example 2 evaluated exactly this exponential using σx2=I^\sigma_{x}^{2}=\hat Iσx2​=I^ and got cos⁡ϑ I^−isin⁡ϑ σx\cos\vartheta\,\hat I-\ii\sin\vartheta\,\sigma_{x}cosϑI^−isinϑσx​ with ϑ=Δt/ℏ\vartheta=\Delta t/\hbarϑ=Δt/ℏ. The quarter period is ϑ=π/4\vartheta=\pi/4ϑ=π/4, giving

V^  ≡  e−iπσx/4  =  12(1−i−i1). \hat V \;\equiv\; \ee^{-\ii\pi\sigma_{x}/4} \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & -\ii\\ -\ii & 1\end{pmatrix}. V^≡e−iπσx​/4=2​1​(1−i​−i1​).

Unitary, since V^†V^=12(1ii1)(1−i−i1)=I^\hat V^{\dagger}\hat V=\tfrac12\big(\begin{smallmatrix}1&\ii\\ \ii&1\end{smallmatrix}\big)\big(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-\ii\\ -\ii&1\end{smallmatrix}\big)=\hat IV^†V^=21​(1i​i1​)(1−i​−i1​)=I^ ✓, as §7.2 guarantees for any e−iH^t/ℏ\ee^{-\ii\hat Ht/\hbar}e−iH^t/ℏ with H^\hat HH^ Hermitian. Applied to ∣0⟩\ket0∣0⟩ it gives 12(1,−i)\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,-\ii)2​1​(1,−i), whose two probabilities are 12\half21​ and 12\half21​.

(b) Squaring,

V^2  =  12(1−i−i1)(1−i−i1)  =  12(0−2i−2i0)  =  −i σx. \hat V^{2} \;=\; \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&-\ii\\ -\ii&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&-\ii\\ -\ii&1\end{pmatrix} \;=\; \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\ii\\ -2\ii&0\end{pmatrix} \;=\; -\ii\,\sigma_{x}. V^2=21​(1−i​−i1​)(1−i​−i1​)=21​(0−2i​−2i0​)=−iσx​.

That is the NOT gate multiplied by −i-\ii−i, and by P1 an overall factor of modulus one is not there. So V^\hat VV^ applied twice takes ∣0⟩\ket0∣0⟩ to ∣1⟩\ket1∣1⟩ with probability 111. It is a genuine square root of NOT, and it is what the pulse of §10.4 performs after 10 ns10\ \mathrm{ns}10 ns.

(c) Now the classical version. A stochastic process on two states that treats them symmetrically is described by the matrix S=(a1−a1−aa)S=\big(\begin{smallmatrix}a&1-a\\ 1-a&a\end{smallmatrix}\big)S=(a1−a​1−aa​) with 0≤a≤10\le a\le10≤a≤1, meaning "stay with probability aaa, flip with probability 1−a1-a1−a". Two applications give

S2=(a2+(1−a)22a(1−a)2a(1−a)a2+(1−a)2), S^{2} = \begin{pmatrix}a^{2}+(1-a)^{2} & 2a(1-a)\\ 2a(1-a) & a^{2}+(1-a)^{2}\end{pmatrix}, S2=(a2+(1−a)22a(1−a)​2a(1−a)a2+(1−a)2​),

and requiring S2S^{2}S2 to be the certain flip means requiring the diagonal entry a2+(1−a)2a^{2}+(1-a)^{2}a2+(1−a)2 to vanish. It is a sum of two squares of real numbers, so it vanishes only if both vanish, which needs a=0a=0a=0 and a=1a=1a=1 at once. Its minimum over all real aaa is 12\half21​, attained at a=12a=\halfa=21​. No classical two-state process, applied twice, produces a certain flip. The best possible leaves a half chance of being where it started.

(d) The difference is P1's, not P3's. The quantum operator succeeds because the two intermediate amplitudes are 1/21/\sqrt21/2​ and −i/2-\ii/\sqrt2−i/2​, and on the second application the contributions to "stay" are 12\tfrac1221​ and (−i)212=−12(-\ii)^{2}\tfrac12=-\tfrac12(−i)221​=−21​, which cancel. Cancellation requires the entries to be complex numbers of opposite sign, which requires the state to be a vector in a complex space rather than a list of probabilities. Section 5.4 named that as the single place a reader is most likely to install the wrong picture. Half-way through a NOT gate the qubit is not "probably still ∣0⟩\ket0∣0⟩". It is in a definite state whose phase is what makes the second half of the gate work.

Problem 1 — rays, not vectors, and the sphere that follows

(a) Show that the set of states of an nnn-level system has 2n−22n-22n−2 real parameters, and say which constraint removes each of the two. (b) For n=2n=2n=2, show that every state can be written as (4.2.6) for exactly one pair (θ,φ)(\theta,\varphi)(θ,φ) with 0≤θ≤π0\le\theta\le\pi0≤θ≤π and 0≤φ<2π0\le\varphi\lt2\pi0≤φ<2π, treating θ=0\theta=0θ=0 and θ=π\theta=\piθ=π as the two exceptions and saying what happens there. (c) Compute ⟨σx⟩,⟨σy⟩,⟨σz⟩\avg{\sigma_{x}},\avg{\sigma_{y}},\avg{\sigma_{z}}⟨σx​⟩,⟨σy​⟩,⟨σz​⟩ in the state (4.2.6), with σx=(0110)\sigma_{x}=\big(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{smallmatrix}\big)σx​=(01​10​), σy=(0−ii0)\sigma_{y}=\big(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-\ii\\ \ii&0\end{smallmatrix}\big)σy​=(0i​−i0​), σz=(100−1)\sigma_{z}=\big(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\ 0&-1\end{smallmatrix}\big)σz​=(10​0−1​), and identify what the three numbers are. (d) Deduce that two states are the same state exactly when those three expectation values agree, and say why that makes the Bloch sphere a measurement rather than a picture.

Solution

(a) A vector in Cn\C^{n}Cn is 2n2n2n real numbers. The condition ∥ψ∥=1\norm\psi=1∥ψ∥=1 is one real equation, leaving 2n−12n-12n−1. P1 identifies ∣ψ⟩\ket\psi∣ψ⟩ with eiα∣ψ⟩\ee^{\ii\alpha}\ket\psieiα∣ψ⟩, and α\alphaα is one real parameter, leaving 2n−22n-22n−2. Normalisation removes one, and the global phase removes the other.

(b) Write ∣ψ⟩=c1∣1⟩+c2∣2⟩\ket\psi=c_{1}\ket1+c_{2}\ket2∣ψ⟩=c1​∣1⟩+c2​∣2⟩. Choose the phase freedom to make c1c_{1}c1​ real and non-negative, which fixes α\alphaα uniquely unless c1=0c_{1}=0c1​=0. Then c1=cos⁡(θ/2)c_{1}=\cos(\theta/2)c1​=cos(θ/2) for a unique θ∈[0,π]\theta\in[0,\pi]θ∈[0,π], since cos⁡(θ/2)\cos(\theta/2)cos(θ/2) runs monotonically from 111 to 000 on that range, and ∣c2∣=1−c12=sin⁡(θ/2)\abs{c_{2}}=\sqrt{1-c_{1}^{2}}=\sin(\theta/2)∣c2​∣=1−c12​​=sin(θ/2), so c2=eiφsin⁡(θ/2)c_{2}=\ee^{\ii\varphi}\sin(\theta/2)c2​=eiφsin(θ/2) with φ\varphiφ unique modulo 2π2\pi2π. The exceptions are the poles. At θ=0\theta=0θ=0 we have c2=0c_{2}=0c2​=0 and φ\varphiφ is undefined, and at θ=π\theta=\piθ=π we have c1=0c_{1}=0c1​=0 and φ\varphiφ is the leftover phase, which P1 discards. Both are single states, and they are exactly the two points where a polar coordinate system on a sphere degenerates. The parameter count is right, and the coordinates are the ones misbehaving.

(c) With c1=cos⁡(θ/2)c_{1}=\cos(\theta/2)c1​=cos(θ/2), c2=eiφsin⁡(θ/2)c_{2}=\ee^{\ii\varphi}\sin(\theta/2)c2​=eiφsin(θ/2) and (4.2.9),

⟨σz⟩=∣c1∣2−∣c2∣2=cos⁡2θ2−sin⁡2θ2=cos⁡θ, \avg{\sigma_{z}} = \abs{c_{1}}^{2}-\abs{c_{2}}^{2} = \cos^{2}\tfrac\theta2-\sin^{2}\tfrac\theta2 = \cos\theta, ⟨σz​⟩=∣c1​∣2−∣c2​∣2=cos22θ​−sin22θ​=cosθ, ⟨σx⟩=cˉ1c2+cˉ2c1=2Re⁡(cˉ1c2)=2cos⁡θ2sin⁡θ2cos⁡φ=sin⁡θcos⁡φ, \avg{\sigma_{x}} = \bar c_{1}c_{2}+\bar c_{2}c_{1} = 2\operatorname{Re}\big(\bar c_{1}c_{2}\big) = 2\cos\tfrac\theta2\sin\tfrac\theta2\cos\varphi = \sin\theta\cos\varphi, ⟨σx​⟩=cˉ1​c2​+cˉ2​c1​=2Re(cˉ1​c2​)=2cos2θ​sin2θ​cosφ=sinθcosφ,

and the same computation with σy\sigma_{y}σy​ gives −2Im⁡(cˉ1c2)-2\operatorname{Im}(\bar c_{1}c_{2})−2Im(cˉ1​c2​) with the sign convention above, which is sin⁡θsin⁡φ\sin\theta\sin\varphisinθsinφ. So the three expectation values are the Cartesian coordinates of the point at polar angle θ\thetaθ and azimuth φ\varphiφ on the unit sphere. Check the length: sin⁡2θcos⁡2φ+sin⁡2θsin⁡2φ+cos⁡2θ=1\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\varphi+\sin^{2}\theta\sin^{2}\varphi +\cos^{2}\theta=1sin2θcos2φ+sin2θsin2φ+cos2θ=1, so every state sits exactly on the sphere and none inside it. (States inside it exist and are mixtures, which is Chapter 4.11's density operator.)

(d) The map from (θ,φ)(\theta,\varphi)(θ,φ) to the point is a bijection onto the sphere by (b) and (c), so equal expectation values force equal (θ,φ)(\theta,\varphi)(θ,φ) and hence the same state. Each of the three numbers is the average of a measurement, and Chapter 4.8 measures exactly these with three Stern–Gerlach magnets in three orientations. So the position of a state on the sphere is determined by an experiment, and the sphere is where the states are rather than a way of imagining them. Note that this fails for n≥3n\ge3n≥3. The parameter count gives four real parameters, there is no two-sphere, and no comparable picture exists.

Problem 2 — how the ammonia maser sorts its molecules

Put the molecule of §10.2 in a uniform electric field E\mathcal{E}E. The two configurations ∣L⟩\ket L∣L⟩ and ∣R⟩\ket R∣R⟩ have electric dipole moments of magnitude μ\muμ pointing in opposite directions along the symmetry axis, so the field shifts their energies by ∓μE\mp\mu\mathcal{E}∓μE: the matrix is (4.2.31) with δ=μE\delta=\mu\mathcal{E}δ=μE and Δ\DeltaΔ unchanged. (a) Write down the two energies as functions of E\mathcal{E}E and sketch their behaviour at small and large field. (b) Find the field at which the two régimes cross over, and evaluate it for μ=1.4718 D=4.909×10−30 C m\mu=1.4718\ \mathrm{D}=4.909\times10^{-30}\ \mathrm{C\,m}μ=1.4718 D=4.909×10−30 Cm. (c) Explain, from (a), why passing a beam through an inhomogeneous field separates the two energy eigenstates, and which way each is deflected. (d) What happens to the inversion oscillation of (4.2.37) as the field is raised?

Solution

(a) Straight from (4.2.32),

E±(E)  =  Eˉ±Δ2+μ2E2. E_{\pm}(\mathcal{E}) \;=\; \bar E \pm\sqrt{\Delta^{2}+\mu^{2}\mathcal{E}^{2}}. E±​(E)=Eˉ±Δ2+μ2E2​.

At small field, expand: Δ2+μ2E2=Δ(1+μ2E2/2Δ2+⋯)\sqrt{\Delta^{2}+\mu^{2}\mathcal{E}^{2}} =\Delta\big(1+\mu^{2}\mathcal{E}^{2}/2\Delta^{2}+\cdots\big)Δ2+μ2E2​=Δ(1+μ2E2/2Δ2+⋯), so the shift is quadratic in E\mathcal{E}E with coefficient ±μ2/2Δ\pm\mu^{2}/2\Delta±μ2/2Δ. At large field the square root is dominated by μE\mu\mathcal{E}μE and the shift is linear, ±μE\pm\mu\mathcal{E}±μE, which is the classical answer for a dipole in a field. The two levels never cross. They repel to a minimum separation of 2Δ2\Delta2Δ at zero field, which is the avoided crossing of §10.1.

(b) The crossover is where the two terms under the root are equal, μE=Δ\mu\mathcal{E}=\DeltaμE=Δ. With Δ=12hν0=7.908×10−24 J\Delta=\half h\nu_{0}=7.908\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{J}Δ=21​hν0​=7.908×10−24 J,

E×=Δμ=7.908×10−244.909×10−30=1.611×106 V m−1=16.1 kV cm−1. \mathcal{E}_{\times} = \frac{\Delta}{\mu} = \frac{7.908\times10^{-24}}{4.909\times10^{-30}} = 1.611\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}} = 16.1\ \mathrm{kV\,cm^{-1}}. E×​=μΔ​=4.909×10−307.908×10−24​=1.611×106 Vm−1=16.1 kVcm−1.

At 1 kV cm−11\ \mathrm{kV\,cm^{-1}}1 kVcm−1 the splitting has grown by only 0.19%0.19\%0.19%. At 100 kV cm−1100\ \mathrm{kV\,cm^{-1}}100 kVcm−1 it has grown by a factor of 6.296.296.29, and the response is essentially linear.

(c) An inhomogeneous field exerts a force −∇E±(E(x))-\nabla E_{\pm}(\mathcal{E}(\vv x))−∇E±​(E(x)) on a molecule in the corresponding state. Since E+E_{+}E+​ increases with field strength and E−E_{-}E−​ decreases, the upper state is pushed towards weak field and the lower state towards strong field. They go opposite ways, and a quadrupole field with a minimum on the axis focuses the upper state down the axis while throwing the lower state out. That is the maser's state selector, and what emerges is a beam of molecules in the upper energy state only. That is a population inversion, which Chapter 4.1's Worked example 3 proved cannot occur in thermal equilibrium at any temperature, and which therefore has to be manufactured.

(d) By (4.2.35) the oscillation amplitude is sin⁡22θ=Δ2/(Δ2+μ2E2)\sin^{2}2\theta=\Delta^{2}/(\Delta^{2}+\mu^{2}\mathcal{E}^{2})sin22θ=Δ2/(Δ2+μ2E2), which falls as the field rises, while the frequency 2R/h2R/h2R/h rises. At E≫E×\mathcal{E}\gg\mathcal{E}_{\times}E≫E×​ the amplitude goes as (Δ/μE)2(\Delta/\mu\mathcal{E})^{2}(Δ/μE)2 and the molecule is essentially frozen into whichever configuration it started in, because the field has made the two configurations energetically distinguishable by far more than the tunnelling can bridge. A strong field switches the inversion off, and this is the same mechanism by which a large molecule's environment freezes it into one enantiomer.

Problem 3 — how badly a finite matrix misses the canonical commutator

Section 8.3 asserted a bound. Prove it and interpret it. (a) Using the inner product ⟨A,B⟩=tr⁡(A†B)\avg{A,B}=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\dagger}B)⟨A,B⟩=tr(A†B) on n×nn\times nn×n complex matrices, which is Chapter 0.5 §1.2's fifth row, verify the three axioms hold, and compute ∥I^∥F\norm{\hat I}_{F}​I^​F​. (b) Prove ∣tr⁡M∣≤n ∥M∥F\abs{\operatorname{tr}M}\le\sqrt n\,\norm{M}_{F}∣trM∣≤n​∥M∥F​ for every MMM, and state which theorem of Chapter 0.5 you used. (c) Deduce ∥[X^,P^]−iℏI^∥F≥ℏn\norm{[\hat X,\hat P]-\ii\hbar\hat I}_{F}\ge\hbar\sqrt n​[X^,P^]−iℏI^​F​≥ℏn​ for all n×nn\times nn×n matrices X^,P^\hat X,\hat PX^,P^, and say what the right-hand side is the norm of. (d) Determine exactly when equality holds, using Chapter 0.5 §1.4's equality condition, and say what that means about how close a finite-dimensional model can get. Check your answer against the pair X^=(0100)\hat X=\big(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\ 0&0\end{smallmatrix}\big)X^=(00​10​), P^=ℏ(00i0)\hat P=\hbar\big(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\ \ii&0\end{smallmatrix}\big)P^=ℏ(0i​00​).

Solution

(a) Conjugate symmetry: tr⁡(A†B)‾=tr⁡((A†B)†)=tr⁡(B†A)\overline{\operatorname{tr}(A^{\dagger}B)} =\operatorname{tr}\big((A^{\dagger}B)^{\dagger}\big)=\operatorname{tr}(B^{\dagger}A)tr(A†B)​=tr((A†B)†)=tr(B†A), since the trace of the conjugate transpose is the conjugate of the trace. Linearity in the second slot is linearity of the trace. Positive definiteness: tr⁡(A†A)=∑i(A†A)ii=∑i,jAji‾Aji=∑ij∣Aij∣2≥0\operatorname{tr}(A^{\dagger}A)=\sum_{i}(A^{\dagger}A)_{ii} =\sum_{i,j}\overline{A_{ji}}A_{ji}=\sum_{ij}\abs{A_{ij}}^{2}\ge0tr(A†A)=∑i​(A†A)ii​=∑i,j​Aji​​Aji​=∑ij​∣Aij​∣2≥0, vanishing only if every entry does. And ∥I^∥F2=tr⁡I^=n\norm{\hat I}_{F}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}\hat I=n​I^​F2​=trI^=n, so ∥I^∥F=n\norm{\hat I}_{F}=\sqrt n​I^​F​=n​.

(b) tr⁡M=tr⁡(I^†M)=⟨I^,M⟩\operatorname{tr}M=\operatorname{tr}(\hat I^{\dagger}M)=\avg{\hat I,M}trM=tr(I^†M)=⟨I^,M⟩, so Cauchy–Schwarz (Chapter 0.5 §1.4) applied in this inner-product space gives ∣⟨I^,M⟩∣2≤⟨I^,I^⟩⟨M,M⟩=n∥M∥F2\abs{\avg{\hat I,M}}^{2}\le\avg{\hat I,\hat I}\avg{M,M}=n\norm{M}_{F}^{2}​⟨I^,M⟩​2≤⟨I^,I^⟩⟨M,M⟩=n∥M∥F2​. Take square roots. The point worth noticing is that Chapter 0.5 proved Cauchy–Schwarz from the three axioms alone and never mentioned what the vectors were, so it applies verbatim to a space whose vectors are matrices.

(c) Put M=[X^,P^]−iℏI^M=[\hat X,\hat P]-\ii\hbar\hat IM=[X^,P^]−iℏI^. By cyclicity of the trace (Chapter 0.4 §6.1) the commutator is traceless, so tr⁡M=−iℏn\operatorname{tr}M=-\ii\hbar ntrM=−iℏn and ∣tr⁡M∣=ℏn\abs{\operatorname{tr}M}=\hbar n∣trM∣=ℏn. Then (b) gives ℏn≤n ∥M∥F\hbar n\le\sqrt n\,\norm{M}_{F}ℏn≤n​∥M∥F​, that is ∥M∥F≥ℏn\norm{M}_{F}\ge\hbar\sqrt n∥M∥F​≥ℏn​. The right-hand side is exactly ∥iℏI^∥F=ℏ∥I^∥F=ℏn\norm{\ii\hbar\hat I}_{F}=\hbar\norm{\hat I}_{F}=\hbar\sqrt n​iℏI^​F​=ℏ​I^​F​=ℏn​: the error is at least as big as the target.

(d) Chapter 0.5 §1.4 proved that Cauchy–Schwarz is an equality exactly when the two vectors are parallel, so equality here needs M=cI^M=c\hat IM=cI^ for some complex ccc. Taking the trace, cn=tr⁡M=−iℏncn=\operatorname{tr}M=-\ii\hbar ncn=trM=−iℏn, so c=−iℏc=-\ii\hbarc=−iℏ and

[X^,P^]−iℏI^=−iℏI^⟺[X^,P^]=0. \big[\hat X,\hat P\big]-\ii\hbar\hat I = -\ii\hbar\hat I \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \big[\hat X,\hat P\big]=0. [X^,P^]−iℏI^=−iℏI^⟺[X^,P^]=0.

The bound is attained exactly when the two matrices commute, which is to say when they reproduce none of the canonical relation whatever. Every pair that actually tries, by having a non-zero commutator, does strictly worse. Check it on the suggested pair. We have X^P^=ℏdiag⁡(i,0)\hat X\hat P=\hbar\operatorname{diag}(\ii,0)X^P^=ℏdiag(i,0) and P^X^=ℏdiag⁡(0,i)\hat P\hat X=\hbar\operatorname{diag}(0,\ii)P^X^=ℏdiag(0,i), so [X^,P^]=iℏdiag⁡(1,−1)[\hat X,\hat P]=\ii\hbar\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)[X^,P^]=iℏdiag(1,−1), which has half of it exactly right. Then M=iℏdiag⁡(0,−2)M=\ii\hbar\operatorname{diag}(0,-2)M=iℏdiag(0,−2) with ∥M∥F=2ℏ\norm{M}_{F}=2\hbar∥M∥F​=2ℏ, a relative error of 2ℏ/(ℏ2)=1.4142\hbar/(\hbar\sqrt2)=1.4142ℏ/(ℏ2​)=1.414 against the commuting pair's 1.0001.0001.000. Getting one diagonal entry exactly right cost more than giving up did.

So there is no sequence of finite-dimensional models converging to the canonical commutator, not even slowly: the relative error is bounded below by 111 at every dimension, and the minimum is achieved by doing nothing. Numerical minimisation over all complex n×nn\times nn×n pairs from twelve random starts returns 1.0000001.0000001.000000 at n=2,3,4,5n=2,3,4,5n=2,3,4,5, which is the bound and its equality case, found without being told about either.

Problem 4 — design a neutrino experiment

The other mass splitting is Δm212=7.53×10−5 eV2\Delta m^{2}_{21}=7.53\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV^{2}}Δm212​=7.53×10−5 eV2 with sin⁡22θ12=0.851\sin^{2}2\theta_{12}=0.851sin22θ12​=0.851. Reactors emit electron antineutrinos with energies of a few MeV; take E=4 MeVE=4\ \mathrm{MeV}E=4 MeV. (a) Using (4.2.43), find the baseline at which the disappearance is greatest, and the oscillation length. (b) The KamLAND experiment used reactors at an average of about 180 km180\ \mathrm{km}180 km. Compute the survival probability there at 4 MeV4\ \mathrm{MeV}4 MeV and say where on the oscillation curve that sits. (c) Daya Bay, measuring the other angle, is at 1.65 km1.65\ \mathrm{km}1.65 km. Show that this is the right baseline for Δm312\Delta m^{2}_{31}Δm312​ and the wrong one for Δm212\Delta m^{2}_{21}Δm212​, with numbers. (d) A colleague proposes measuring Δm212\Delta m^{2}_{21}Δm212​ with a detector 100 m100\ \mathrm{m}100 m from a reactor, arguing that being closer means more neutrinos. Say quantitatively why this fails.

Solution

(a) Maximum disappearance is the first maximum of sin⁡2\sin^{2}sin2, at phase π/2\pi/2π/2:

Oscillation experiments are placed by (4.2.44) and not by flux.

Problem 5 — entanglement, by counting

(a) Show that the four-dimensional space of two two-level systems contains states that are not of the form ∣ϕ⟩⊗∣χ⟩\ket\phi\otimes\ket\chi∣ϕ⟩⊗∣χ⟩, by exhibiting one and proving no factorisation exists. (b) A general two-qubit state is c00∣00⟩+c01∣01⟩+c10∣10⟩+c11∣11⟩c_{00}\ket{00}+c_{01}\ket{01}+c_{10}\ket{10}+c_{11}\ket{11}c00​∣00⟩+c01​∣01⟩+c10​∣10⟩+c11​∣11⟩. Show that it factorises if and only if c00c11=c01c10c_{00}c_{11}=c_{01}c_{10}c00​c11​=c01​c10​, and interpret that as one complex condition on four complex numbers. (c) Confirm §9.2's parameter count for m=n=2m=n=2m=n=2 using (b), remembering P1. (d) For ∣Ψ⟩=12(∣00⟩+∣11⟩)\ket\Psi=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00}+\ket{11})∣Ψ⟩=2​1​(∣00⟩+∣11⟩), compute the probabilities of the four outcomes of measuring σz\sigma_{z}σz​ on both systems, and then the two outcomes of measuring σz\sigma_{z}σz​ on the first system alone. Say what is strange about the answer and which chapter handles it.

Solution

(a) Take ∣Ψ⟩=12(∣00⟩+∣11⟩)\ket\Psi=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00}+\ket{11})∣Ψ⟩=2​1​(∣00⟩+∣11⟩) and suppose ∣Ψ⟩=(a∣0⟩+b∣1⟩)⊗(c∣0⟩+d∣1⟩)\ket\Psi=(a\ket0+b\ket1)\otimes(c\ket0+d\ket1)∣Ψ⟩=(a∣0⟩+b∣1⟩)⊗(c∣0⟩+d∣1⟩). Expanding by (4.2.28) and matching the four coefficients gives (4.2.29): ac=bd=1/2ac=bd=1/\sqrt2ac=bd=1/2​ and ad=bc=0ad=bc=0ad=bc=0. From ad=0ad=0ad=0, either a=0a=0a=0, which contradicts ac=1/2ac=1/\sqrt2ac=1/2​, or d=0d=0d=0, which contradicts bd=1/2bd=1/\sqrt2bd=1/2​. No factorisation exists.

(b) If the state factorises then cij=ϕiχjc_{ij}=\phi_{i}\chi_{j}cij​=ϕi​χj​ and c00c11=ϕ0χ0ϕ1χ1=c01c10c_{00}c_{11}=\phi_{0}\chi_{0}\phi_{1}\chi_{1}=c_{01}c_{10}c00​c11​=ϕ0​χ0​ϕ1​χ1​=c01​c10​, so the condition is necessary. Conversely suppose c00c11=c01c10c_{00}c_{11}=c_{01}c_{10}c00​c11​=c01​c10​. If c00≠0c_{00}\neq0c00​=0, set ϕ0=1\phi_{0}=1ϕ0​=1, ϕ1=c10/c00\phi_{1}=c_{10}/c_{00}ϕ1​=c10​/c00​, χ0=c00\chi_{0}=c_{00}χ0​=c00​, χ1=c01\chi_{1}=c_{01}χ1​=c01​. Then ϕ0χ0=c00\phi_{0}\chi_{0}=c_{00}ϕ0​χ0​=c00​ ✓, ϕ0χ1=c01\phi_{0}\chi_{1}=c_{01}ϕ0​χ1​=c01​ ✓, ϕ1χ0=c10\phi_{1}\chi_{0}=c_{10}ϕ1​χ0​=c10​ ✓, and ϕ1χ1=c10c01/c00=c11\phi_{1}\chi_{1}=c_{10}c_{01}/c_{00}=c_{11}ϕ1​χ1​=c10​c01​/c00​=c11​ by hypothesis ✓. If c00=0c_{00}=0c00​=0 the same argument runs from whichever coefficient is non-zero. So factorising is exactly the vanishing of the 2×22\times22×2 determinant c00c11−c01c10c_{00}c_{11}-c_{01}c_{10}c00​c11​−c01​c10​. That is one complex equation on four complex numbers, which is a two-real-dimensional condition, and it confirms that product states are a thin set rather than a large one.

(c) Product states satisfy one complex equation inside C4\C^{4}C4, so they form a set of complex dimension 3=m+n−13=m+n-13=m+n−1 with m=n=2m=n=2m=n=2, exactly §9.2's count. Now count them as states. Imposing ∥Ψ∥=1\norm\Psi=1∥Ψ∥=1 and discarding the global phase removes two real dimensions, by Problem 1(a). So the whole space has 2×4−2=62\times4-2=62×4−2=6 real parameters and the product states have 2×3−2=42\times3-2=42×3−2=4, which is also 2+22+22+2: two real parameters for each qubit's own Bloch sphere, as it must be.

(d) The joint measurement projects onto the four basis states, and by P3 the probabilities are ∣cij∣2\abs{c_{ij}}^{2}∣cij​∣2: Pr⁡(00)=Pr⁡(11)=12\Pr(00)=\Pr(11)=\halfPr(00)=Pr(11)=21​ and Pr⁡(01)=Pr⁡(10)=0\Pr(01)=\Pr(10)=0Pr(01)=Pr(10)=0. Measuring only the first system means measuring σz⊗I^\sigma_{z}\otimes\hat Iσz​⊗I^, whose eigenvalue +1+1+1 has the two-dimensional eigenspace spanned by ∣00⟩,∣01⟩\ket{00},\ket{01}∣00⟩,∣01⟩. By P3 in its projection form, Pr⁡(+1)=∥P^+∣Ψ⟩∥2=12\Pr(+1)=\norm{\hat P_{+}\ket\Psi}^{2}=\halfPr(+1)=​P^+​∣Ψ⟩​2=21​ and likewise Pr⁡(−1)=12\Pr(-1)=\halfPr(−1)=21​.

What is strange is the combination. Each system on its own is completely unpredictable, a fair coin, and yet the two always agree. There is no state of the first system alone that reproduces this. Assigning it ∣0⟩\ket0∣0⟩ or ∣1⟩\ket1∣1⟩ contradicts the observed randomness, and assigning it any superposition contradicts (a). The description "each has a definite but unknown value, correlated at preparation" reproduces these particular numbers and is ruled out by measuring other observables, which is the content of Bell's inequality. Chapter 4.11 builds the density operator to answer "what is the first system's state" and then measures the inequality.

The brick you just laid — and the two chapters it forces

The table was the chapter. Twenty-two rows, every left-hand entry a theorem of Chapter 0.5 cited at the section that states it, every right-hand entry that theorem with two or three words changed. Real measured values are 0.5 §6.1. Perfectly distinguishable outcomes are §6.2, and the confusion probability is exactly zero rather than small. Any state being a superposition of the outcomes of any observable is §6.3. Probabilities adding to one is Parseval, §2. Compatible measurements and the quantum numbers that label a state are §8. Symmetries and evolution generated by observables are §7.1. None of that was assumed here and none of it was re-proved here, which was the instruction.

Seven assertions, boxed and flagged, and they are the whole of the addition.

  • A state is a unit ray, so that normalisation makes Parseval read as probability and the overall phase drops out of every prediction by one line of conjugation. The relative phase between terms is the opposite case. It produces cos⁡2(β/2)\cos^{2}(\beta/2)cos2(β/2), and it is the entire wave behaviour of Chapter 4.1 §6.6, now living somewhere definite.
  • An observable is Hermitian, which is the only postulate the measurement outcomes need. Chapter 4.4 §4 will sharpen it to self-adjoint for a physical reason: momentum on a half-line has no self-adjoint extension and is therefore not an observable.
  • The Born rule, which is not derivable, is still open, and was marked as such at the moment it entered rather than afterwards. Gleason's theorem was quoted with its hypotheses and explicitly not presented as a derivation.
  • The state update is a separate postulate, and Worked example 1 shows why the separation is not bookkeeping. Three magnets give 12\tfrac1221​ when the middle one is read, and exactly 000 when it is not.
  • The generator of time evolution is the energy, which is the only new content in §7. Unitarity followed from probability conservation in three lines, and the existence of a Hermitian generator followed from unitarity in three more.
  • The canonical commutator is postulated here rather than in Chapter 4.7, because Chapters 4.5, 4.6 and 4.8 all need it first.
  • And a composite system's space is the tensor product, so dimensions multiply.

Three lines that settle the shape of the book. The trace of a commutator is zero by cyclicity, from Chapter 0.4 §6.1. The trace of iℏI^n\ii\hbar\hat I_{n}iℏI^n​ is iℏn\ii\hbar niℏn. So no finite matrices satisfy [x^,p^]=iℏI^[\hat x,\hat p]=\ii\hbar\hat I[x^,p^​]=iℏI^. Cauchy–Schwarz in the matrix inner product sharpens that: ∥[x^,p^]−iℏI^∥F≥ℏn=∥iℏI^∥F\norm{[\hat x,\hat p]-\ii\hbar\hat I}_{F}\ge\hbar\sqrt n=\norm{\ii\hbar\hat I}_{F}​[x^,p^​]−iℏI^​F​≥ℏn​=​iℏI^​F​ at every dimension, with equality exactly for commuting pairs. So a finite model's best strategy is to reproduce none of the relation, and direct numerical minimisation confirms the ratio 1.0000001.0000001.000000 at n=2,3,4,5n=2,3,4,5n=2,3,4,5. Quantum mechanics is infinite-dimensional before a single physical question has been asked, and the proof needs nothing but a trace.

And one matrix did all three systems. With H^\hat HH^ having mean Eˉ\bar EEˉ, difference δ\deltaδ and coupling Δ\DeltaΔ, the splitting is 2δ2+Δ22\sqrt{\delta^{2}+\Delta^{2}}2δ2+Δ2​ and P1→2=sin⁡22θ sin⁡2(ΔE t/2ℏ)P_{1\to2}=\sin^{2}2\theta\,\sin^{2}(\Delta E\,t/2\hbar)P1→2​=sin22θsin2(ΔEt/2ℏ), with Eˉ\bar EEˉ absent because it is a global phase. Read once: ammonia, δ=0\delta=0δ=0 by mirror symmetry, splitting h×23.8701 GHz=98.72 μeVh\times23.8701\ \mathrm{GHz} =98.72\ \mu\mathrm{eV}h×23.8701 GHz=98.72 μeV, inversion period 41.89 ps41.89\ \mathrm{ps}41.89 ps, wavelength 1.256 cm1.256\ \mathrm{cm}1.256 cm, stimulated emission favoured over spontaneous by 261261261 at room temperature. That is the maser, with every design number on the page. Read again with t→L/ct\to L/ct→L/c and ΔE=Δm2c4/2E\Delta E=\Delta m^{2}c^{4}/2EΔE=Δm2c4/2E expanded from Chapter 2.5's dispersion relation: the oscillation formula sin⁡22θsin⁡2(Δm2c4L/4ℏcE)\sin^{2}2\theta\sin^{2}(\Delta m^{2}c^{4}L/4\hbar cE)sin22θsin2(Δm2c4L/4ℏcE), its coefficient 1.266931.266931.26693 derived rather than quoted, and T2K's 295 km295\ \mathrm{km}295 km at 0.600 GeV0.600\ \mathrm{GeV}0.600 GeV sitting at 0.486π0.486\pi0.486π against an oscillation length of 607.3 km607.3\ \mathrm{km}607.3 km. Read a third time with both parameters chosen by an engineer: a 20 ns20\ \mathrm{ns}20 ns NOT gate and a 10 ns10\ \mathrm{ns}10 ns square root of it, which Worked example 3 shows no classical two-state process possesses. The figure integrates the equation numerically and holds ∣c1∣2+∣c2∣2=1\abs{c_{1}}^{2}+\abs{c_{2}}^{2}=1∣c1​∣2+∣c2​∣2=1 to about 10−1410^{-14}10−14 through the whole cycle at every setting, moves not at all under a full turn of the global phase, and shows every detuned curve leaving the origin along the same parabola τ2\tau^{2}τ2, which is the fact Chapter 4.10's transition rate is built on.

Where this gets spent. Ten flags. Seven are the postulates. One is Gleason with its hypotheses. One is the fundamental theorem of algebra inherited from Chapter 0.4 §7, which is the single thing this chapter quotes rather than derives or postulates, and the thing the whole measurement apparatus descends from, paid off in Chapter 5.4. And one is the measured parameters of §10. That is the largest count in the book and it is correct, because this is the only chapter whose subject is the postulates.

What is owed is now precise rather than vague. Chapter 0.5 named the four places its proofs used finite dimension, calling them "in the induction, in rank–nullity, in the interchange of sums, in the claim that an injective map is surjective", and §8 showed that infinite dimension is forced. The bill is paid in two instalments, and the shape repeats one you have already seen: Chapter 0.4 built the space and Chapter 0.5 built the operators on it. Chapter 4.3 builds the space and Chapter 4.4 builds the operators on it.

Chapter 4.3 discards the Riemann integral, builds the Lebesgue integral, proves L2L^{2}L2 complete so that a limit of states is a state, and shows the Fourier modes really are an orthonormal basis. Everything here that said "expand in a basis" is on credit until then. Chapter 4.4 supplies domains, the difference between symmetric and self-adjoint that P2's box warned about, spectra with no eigenvectors in the space, the spectral theorem in the form that survives, Stone's theorem for §7.3, and the meaning of ∣x⟩\ket x∣x⟩ and ∣p⟩\ket p∣p⟩. Everything here that said "the spectral theorem" is on credit until then.

After that, the list gets spent one chapter at a time.

  • Chapter 4.5 turns (4.2.18) into a differential equation and solves it.
  • Chapter 4.6 diagonalises the oscillator, which is §4.2's "solving a system means diagonalising its Hamiltonian".
  • Chapter 4.7 applies Cauchy–Schwarz to (A^−⟨A^⟩)∣ψ⟩(\hat A-\avg{\hat A})\ket\psi(A^−⟨A^⟩)∣ψ⟩ and (B^−⟨B^⟩)∣ψ⟩(\hat B-\avg{\hat B})\ket\psi(B^−⟨B^⟩)∣ψ⟩ and gets the uncertainty principle with nothing added, then proves that P6 cannot be extended to every observable.
  • Chapter 4.8 spends §4.3's quantum numbers on angular momentum.
  • Chapter 4.11 returns to P3, P4 and P7 together, which is where the three of them turn out to have been the interesting ones all along.
